query.original_query: reasoning models overthinking efficiency internal signal token allocation numeric format

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal reasoning signal token allocation and overthinking in large language models, efficiency of intermediate reasoning tokens, representation of numeric format and chain-of-thought
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the allocation of internal reasoning signals in large language models during chain-of-thought generation, focusing on the phenomenon of overthinking where models allocate excessive intermediate tokens without proportional gains in accuracy. Our analysis examines how numeric format representation—including digit tokenization and decimal placement—influences the efficiency of intermediate reasoning steps. Using activation patching and causal tracing, we localize reasoning-critical computations to specific attention heads and MLP layers within the residual stream, finding that many intermediate tokens contribute minimally to final answer derivation. We further analyze the relationship between token-level feature activation and reasoning path length, revealing that models often maintain redundant representations of numeric values across multiple steps. Results show that pruning intermediate tokens based on attention entropy and feature attribution scores can reduce token usage while preserving task performance. Our findings suggest that current autoregressive architectures lack mechanisms to dynamically terminate reasoning, leading to systematic over-allocation of computational resources to intermediate chain-of-thought tokens.

sub_queries.semantic_query: overthinking and reasoning efficiency in human cognition, internal signal for metacognitive control of deliberation, resource allocation in multi-step reasoning, numerical format processing
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated whether the format in which numerical information is presented modulates the efficiency of multi-step reasoning and the metacognitive control of deliberation. Participants completed a series of algebraic reasoning problems presented in either symbolic (Arabic numerals) or verbal (English number words) formats while we measured response times, accuracy, and self-reported confidence. We hypothesized that less fluent formats would increase subjective difficulty, triggering a metacognitive signal to reduce overthinking and allocate cognitive resources more sparingly. Results indicate that verbal-format problems elicited longer deliberation times and lower confidence ratings, yet accuracy did not differ significantly between conditions. Critically, individual differences in the tendency to overthink—measured via a self-report scale—predicted a greater discrepancy in deliberation time between formats. Findings support the hypothesis that metacognitive control of deliberation is sensitive to the fluency of input representation, and that resource allocation in multi-step reasoning is calibrated by an internal signal of processing ease, rather than by objective problem complexity alone.

papers.title: Exploring and Exploiting the Inherent Efficiency within Large Reasoning Models for Self-Guided Efficiency Enhancement
papers.research_question: Can the inherent efficiency within large reasoning models be exploited to reduce overthinking and enhance reasoning efficiency without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that large reasoning models inherently possess untapped efficiency potential, and proposes two self-guided methods—Efficiency Steering (a training-free activation steering technique) and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL (a reinforcement learning framework)—that significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance.
papers.conclusion: Overthinking in large reasoning models is a controllable behavior embedded in internal representations; the proposed self-guided methods (Efficiency Steering and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL) successfully enhance reasoning efficiency without external supervision, offering practical directions for building more cost-efficient reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LRMs exhibit inherent efficiency: the shortest correct reasoning paths are often less than half the length of the longest correct ones, indicating substantial untapped efficiency potential.
Efficient and verbose reasoning paths are linearly separable in the model's representation space, with consistent positional shifts across layers and difficulty levels.
Efficiency Steering, a training-free method that injects a single vector direction derived from contrastive reasoning pairs, can controllably modulate reasoning length without compromising accuracy.
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, which uses a dynamic reward function balancing correctness and brevity, significantly reduces reasoning length while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on simpler mathematical problems (Levels 1-3) leads to efficient reasoning that transfers well to harder problems, suggesting that efficiency priors learned from simple data are effective.
papers.limitation:
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL is sensitive to optimization steps; beyond 30 steps, efficiency improves but correctness can deteriorate, indicating a trade-off that requires careful tuning.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on harder mathematical examples (Levels 4-5) does not yield as favorable efficiency outcomes as training on simpler examples, suggesting that data distribution impacts the method's effectiveness.
future_direction: Further exploration of representational properties of LLMs to build efficiency-aware alignment strategies with minimal external supervision.
Investigating curriculum-aware or simplicity-biased training strategies for self-rewarded efficiency optimization, as simpler problems may provide better efficiency outcomes at lower training cost.
Refining the capabilities that already exist within LRMs for building more efficient and accessible reasoning systems.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced language models' capabilities in complex problem-solving by emulating human-like deliberative thinking. However, these models often exhibit overthinking (i.e., the generation of unnecessarily verbose and redundant content), which hinders efficiency and inflates inference cost. In this work, we explore the representational and behavioral origins of this inefficiency, revealing that LRMs inherently possess the capacity for more concise reasoning. Empirical analyses show that correct reasoning paths vary significantly in length, and the shortest correct responses often suffice, indicating untapped efficiency potential. Exploiting these findings, we propose two lightweight methods to enhance LRM efficiency. First, we introduce Efficiency Steering, a training-free activation steering technique that modulates reasoning behavior via a single direction in the model's representation space. Second, we develop Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically balances task accuracy and brevity by rewarding concise correct solutions. Extensive experiments on seven LRM backbones across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our methods significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance. Our results highlight that reasoning efficiency can be improved by leveraging and guiding the intrinsic capabilities of existing models in a self-guided manner.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Tokens are Computer Program Variables
papers.research_question: What is the role of CoT tokens in LLMs for compositional reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT tokens function like variables in computer programs, storing intermediate values that are used in subsequent computations and are causally related to the final output.
papers.conclusion: CoT tokens behave like variables in computer programs, storing intermediate values that are causally connected to the output, but models may learn shortcuts and there is a computational complexity limit.
papers.key_findings:
CoT is essential for solving compositional problems like multi-digit multiplication and dynamic programming.
Removing non-result tokens (keeping only intermediate results) does not harm performance, indicating that intermediate results are the key.
Intermediate results can be stored in different forms (e.g., latent tokens) without performance drop, unless compression exceeds a complexity limit.
Intervening on CoT token values changes subsequent reasoning and final output, showing causal relation.
Models sometimes take shortcuts in easy subproblems, making interventions fail.
papers.limitation:
No theoretical proof is provided for the hypothesis that CoT tokens function like variables.
Experiments are conducted on two synthetic tasks with one model (Qwen-2.5-1.5B), and not on real-world datasets.
future_direction: Generalization ability of CoT programs.
Identification of intermediate variable tokens in general tasks.
Estimation of computational complexity between variable tokens.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thoughts (CoT) requires large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate steps before reaching the final answer, and has been proven effective to help LLMs solve complex reasoning tasks. However, the inner mechanism of CoT still remains largely unclear. In this paper, we empirically study the role of CoT tokens in LLMs on two compositional tasks: multi-digit multiplication and dynamic programming. While CoT is essential for solving these problems, we find that preserving only tokens that store intermediate results would achieve comparable performance. Furthermore, we observe that storing intermediate results in an alternative latent form will not affect model performance. We also randomly intervene some values in CoT, and notice that subsequent CoT tokens and the final answer would change correspondingly. These findings suggest that CoT tokens may function like variables in computer programs but with potential drawbacks like unintended shortcuts and computational complexity limits between tokens. The code and data are available at https://github.com/solitaryzero/CoTs_are_Variables.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Chain-of-Thought: A Latent Computational Mode in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of Chain-of-Thought prompting in triggering reasoning in large language models? Is CoT the unique mechanism or just one of several triggers for a latent reasoning capability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning in LLMs can be triggered by steering latent internal features identified via Sparse Autoencoders, indicating that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not the unique pathway but one of several triggers for an underlying reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in large language models can be triggered by activating latent internal features, showing that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not unique and that activation-level interventions are useful for understanding and controlling reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single reasoning-related latent feature improves reasoning accuracy without explicit Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Early single-feature steering leads to more concise reasoning outputs in large models, matching or exceeding CoT performance with fewer tokens.
The identified reasoning feature is activated early in generation and is associated with entering a reasoning mode rather than predicting answer correctness.
The reasoning feature generalizes across different prompts that encourage reasoning (e.g., 'Explain how', 'Solve carefully'), not just step-by-step prompts.
Random feature steering does not produce similar improvements, confirming the specificity of the identified reasoning-related feature.
papers.limitation: The identified SAE features are not fully disentangled or isolated reasoning mechanisms; conclusions are based on behavioral and intervention-level evidence, not complete mechanistic characterization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear why it works and whether it is the unique mechanism for triggering reasoning in large language models. In this work, we study this question by directly analyzing and intervening on the internal representations of LLMs with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), identifying a small set of latent features that are causally associated with LLM reasoning behavior. Across multiple model families and reasoning benchmarks, we find that steering a single reasoning-related latent feature can substantially improve accuracy without explicit CoT prompting. For large models, latent steering achieves performance comparable to standard CoT prompting while producing more efficient outputs. We further observe that this reasoning-oriented internal state is triggered early in generation and can override prompt-level instructions that discourage explicit reasoning. Overall, our results suggest that multi-step reasoning in LLMs is supported by latent internal activations that can be externally activated, while CoT prompting is one effective, but not unique, way of activating this mechanism rather than its necessary cause.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
papers.research_question: Why is chain-of-thought reasoning useful in language models? The paper tests the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that chain-of-thought reasoning is effective when training data has local structure, allowing models to chain accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables not seen together in training.
papers.conclusion: The effectiveness of chain-of-thought reasoning in language models is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias in conditional probability estimation when training data is locally structured.
Free generation, where the model chooses intermediate variables, performs similarly to scaffolded generation with ideal intermediates.
Reasoning does not help when training data is fully observed or has the wrong locality structure.
The combination of locally structured training data and reasoning is more data-efficient than training on fully observed data.
When models fail to estimate conditional probabilities accurately, their estimates tend to match marginal probabilities.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified synthetic setting, which may not fully capture natural language data.
papers.abstract: Humans have a powerful and mysterious capacity to reason. Working through a set of mental steps enables us to make inferences we would not be capable of making directly even though we get no additional data from the world. Similarly, when large language models generate intermediate steps (a chain of thought) before answering a question, they often produce better answers than they would directly. We investigate why and how chain-of-thought reasoning is useful in language models, testing the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly. These training conditions enable the chaining of accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables that were not seen together in training. We prove that there will exist a "reasoning gap", where reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias, for the simple case of an autoregressive density estimator trained on local samples from a chain-structured probabilistic model. We then test our hypothesis experimentally in more complex models, training an autoregressive language model on samples from Bayes nets but only including a subset of variables in each sample. We test language models' ability to match conditional probabilities with and without intermediate reasoning steps, finding that intermediate steps are only helpful when the training data is locally structured with respect to dependencies between variables. The combination of locally structured observations and reasoning is much more data-efficient than training on all variables. Our results illustrate how the effectiveness of reasoning step by step is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.

papers.title: State over Tokens: Characterizing the Role of Reasoning Tokens
papers.research_question: What is the functional role of reasoning tokens in LLMs, given that they are not faithful explanations of the model's reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework, which reframes reasoning tokens as an externalized computational state that enables persistence across stateless generation cycles, explaining how they can drive correct reasoning without being faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens are best understood as an externalized computational state (SoT), which resolves misconceptions about their completeness and shared meaning, and opens new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning tokens are not faithful explanations of the model's internal reasoning process.
Reasoning tokens function as an externalized computational state (SoT), the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles.
The SoT view explains two common misconceptions: the misconception of completeness (tokens externalize only what is necessary for the next cycle) and the misconception of shared meaning (tokens may use model-specific encodings not interpretable by humans).
The tokens inhabit distinct ontological categories: as natural language text for human readers and as a computational substrate for the model.
The SoT framework surfaces new research questions about how LLMs encode and use state through tokens.
future_direction: How do LLMs decide what information to externalize at each cycle?
What information is actually encoded in the state at different points in the sequence?
Do they use consistent encodings across the solution of a problem and across different problems?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate reasoning tokens before their final answer to boost performance on complex tasks. While these sequences seem like human thought processes, empirical evidence reveals that they are not a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning process. To address this gap between appearance and function, we introduce the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework. SoT reframes reasoning tokens not as a linguistic narrative, but as an externalized computational state -- the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles. This explains how the tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation when read as text and surfaces previously overlooked research questions on these tokens. We argue that to truly understand the process that LLMs do, research must move beyond reading the reasoning tokens as text and focus on decoding them as state.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can transformers use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') to perform hidden computation and solve algorithmic tasks they cannot solve without intermediate tokens, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail at without intermediate tokens, showing additional tokens provide computational benefits independent of token meaning, but learning to use filler tokens requires specific, dense supervision.
papers.conclusion: For certain parallelizable problems, transformers achieve improved performance with filler tokens instead of chain-of-thought tokens, meaning intermediate tokens can be used purely for computational capacity rather than faithful serial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve perfect accuracy on 3SUM and high accuracy on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens, while failing without them.
The performance gap between filler and no-filler settings increases with problem complexity (input length and dimension).
Filler token representations encode hidden, task-relevant computation, as shown by fine-tuning experiments.
Learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires training on parallelizable chain-of-thought data; instance-adaptive CoT data does not transfer.
Filler tokens extend transformer expressive power within the complexity class TC0, enabling solution of problems with deep quantifier nesting.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which token-parallelizable, TC0 algorithmic problems arise in natural language contexts.

Investigate whether natural-language text provides adequate supervision for filler-token computation, providing parallelizable supervision rather than non-parallelizable, instance-adaptive chains of thought.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Can Aha Moments Be Fake? Identifying True and Decorative Thinking Steps in Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do LLMs truly think through each verbalized step in their chain-of-thought (CoT)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in chain-of-thought reasoning, revealing that LLMs often interleave true-thinking steps with decorative ones, and identifies a steerable 'TrueThinking' direction in latent space that controls whether a step is internally followed.
papers.conclusion: LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps without performing them internally, challenging the efficiency of LLM reasoning and the trustworthiness of chain-of-thought as a safety-monitoring signal.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs often interleave true-thinking steps (which causally affect the final prediction) and decorative-thinking steps (which have minimal causal influence).
Only a small subset of reasoning steps causally drive the model's prediction; e.g., on AIME, only an average of 2.3% of steps have TTS ≥ 0.7 for Qwen-2.5.
Self-verification steps (aha moments) in CoT can be decorative, meaning the model does not truly check its solution internally.
A linear 'TrueThinking' direction in latent space can mediate whether LLMs internally reason over a verbalized step; steering along this direction forces engagement, while reversing it suppresses step use.
The latent signal controlling step engagement is universal across datasets and model sizes, with intermediate layers (e.g., 15-22 in Qwen) concentrating reasoning-related representations.
future_direction: Future study to explain the mechanisms of CoT reasoning and develop training objectives that reward reliance on true-thinking steps.
In-depth study of the geometry of hidden states and TrueThinking directions in the latent space.
papers.abstract: Large language models can generate long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but it remains unclear whether the verbalized steps reflect the models' internal thinking. In this work, we propose a True Thinking Score (TTS) to quantify the causal contribution of each step in CoT to the model's final prediction. Our experiments show that LLMs often interleave between true-thinking steps (which are genuinely used to compute the final output) and decorative-thinking steps (which give the appearance of reasoning but have minimal causal influence). We reveal that only a small subset of the total reasoning steps causally drive the model's prediction: e.g., on AIME, only an average of 2.3% of reasoning steps in CoT have a TTS >= 0.7 (range: 0-1) for Qwen-2.5. Furthermore, we find that LLMs can be steered to internally follow or disregard specific steps in their verbalized CoT using the identified TrueThinking direction. We highlight that self-verification steps in CoT (i.e., aha moments) can be decorative, while steering along the TrueThinking direction can force internal reasoning over these steps. Overall, our work reveals that LLMs often verbalize reasoning steps without performing them internally, challenging the efficiency of LLM reasoning and the trustworthiness of CoT.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: The First Impression Problem: Internal Bias Triggers Overthinking in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models often exhibit overthinking, characterized by redundant reasoning steps. We identify \emph{internal bias} elicited by the input question as a key trigger of such behavior. Upon encountering a problem, the model immediately forms a preliminary guess about the answer, which we term an internal bias since it may not be explicitly generated, and it arises without systematic reasoning. When this guess conflicts with its subsequent reasoning, the model tends to engage in excessive reflection, resulting in wasted computation. We validate the association between internal bias and overthinking across multiple models and diverse reasoning tasks. To demonstrate the causal relationship more rigorously, we conduct two counterfactual interventions, showing that removing the input question after the model reduces the redundant reasoning across various complex reasoning tasks, and manually injecting bias affects overthinking accordingly. Further interpretability experiments suggest that excessive attention to the input question serves as a key mechanism through which internal bias influences subsequent reasoning trajectories. Finally, we evaluated several methods aimed at mitigating overthinking, yet the influence of internal bias persisted under all conditions.

papers.title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
papers.research_question: Do latent tokens in Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT) actually encode reasoning, or do they merely simulate the appearance of it?
papers.core_contribution: Latent tokens in COCONUT function as uninterpretable placeholders and promote shortcut usage, rather than encoding faithful reasoning, leading to inflated benchmark performance without true reasoning.
papers.conclusion: COCONUT tokens serve as pseudo-reasoning placeholders, are not semantically interpretable, and exhibit shortcut behaviors, indicating that latent reasoning in COCONUT is not faithful.
papers.key_findings:
COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering perturbations (PSR <5%) compared to CoT tokens (PSR up to 50%), indicating they lack reasoning-critical information.
Token-swapping experiments show COCONUT's accuracy remains stable after swapping, while CoT's drops, indicating latent tokens have limited influence on final predictions.
COCONUT exhibits strong shortcut dependence, e.g., in MMLU with biased options, incorrect predictions selecting the biased option rise to 70%.
In HotpotQA, COCONUT shows extreme sensitivity to shortcut manipulation, with accuracy dropping to near 0% when shortcuts favor incorrect answers.
PCA visualizations show latent token embeddings are distributed far from the main vocabulary manifold, indicating they act as placeholders without semantic meaning.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not establish a formal causal link between latent representations and reasoning quality.
The study did not deeply investigate the reasons why COCONUT relies on shortcuts, so the analysis remains speculative.
future_direction: Investigate more challenging out-of-distribution evaluations.
Design reasoning-specialized LLM baselines.
Develop novel interpretability metrics to probe latent reasoning traces.
papers.abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.

papers.title: Think Clearly: Improving Reasoning via Redundant Token Pruning
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have shown promising capabilities in long-form reasoning, following structured chains of thought before arriving at a final answer. However, we observe that these reasoning paths tend to include substantial redundancy; analyzing attention patterns reveals that attention scores are widely scattered, particularly incorrect answers exhibit greater attention sparsity. In this paper, we demonstrate that deliberately removing this redundancy in the reasoning process significantly improves performance through clear thinking, i.e., removing distraction. Specifically, we systematically identify reasoning redundancy by measuring token-level attention scores to a special end-of-thinking token, which is appended to an explicit instruction inserted to conclude each intermediate reasoning step. Furthermore, we propose structure-aware pruning that prioritizes removing tokens in low-contributing reasoning chunks over individual tokens. After evicting redundant tokens, we remove the injected end-of-thinking instruction, then resume the reasoning generation. We demonstrate that our method significantly improves overall accuracy across reasoning-intensive benchmarks without any training involved. In particular, our method shows strong performance on challenging mathematical competition benchmarks such as AIME and AMC, where reasoning redundancy is more prevalent.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting. Swapping a small set of CoT-reasoning features into a noCoT run raises answer log-probabilities significantly in the 2.8B model, but has no reliable effect in 70M, revealing a clear scale threshold. CoT also leads to significantly higher activation sparsity and feature interpretability scores in the larger model, signalling more modular internal computation. For example, the model's confidence in generating correct answers improves from 1.2 to 4.3. We introduce patch-curves and random-feature patching baselines, showing that useful CoT information is not only present in the top-K patches but widely distributed. Overall, our results indicate that CoT can induce more interpretable internal structures in high-capacity LLMs, validating its role as a structured prompting method.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like intuitive reasoning errors, and how do more advanced models avoid these errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs exhibit human-like intuitive errors (System 1), but more advanced models (ChatGPT, GPT-4) avoid these errors through chain-of-thought reasoning and well-developed intuition, performing hyperrationally.
papers.conclusion: Psychological methods can reveal emergent traits in LLMs; advanced LLMs show remarkable reasoning abilities and can avoid intuitive errors, resembling both System 1 and System 2 processes.
papers.key_findings:
Early/smaller LLMs (up to GPT-3-curie) often give atypical responses, indicating poor task comprehension.
Larger pre-ChatGPT models (GPT-3-davinci family) show a high tendency to give intuitive but incorrect responses, similar to human System 1 errors.
ChatGPT models (especially GPT-4) show a high fraction of correct responses, often using chain-of-thought reasoning.
Instructing GPT-3-davinci-003 to use chain-of-thought reasoning reduces intuitive errors and increases correct responses.
Providing training examples (few-shot) improves GPT-3-davinci-003's performance on both CRT and semantic illusions.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested one family of LLMs (the GPT family).
The tasks used are limited in scope (CRT and semantic illusions).
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is not truly deliberate System 2 reasoning but resembles it.
papers.abstract: We design a battery of semantic illusions and cognitive reflection tests, aimed to elicit intuitive yet erroneous responses. We administer these tasks, traditionally used to study reasoning and decision-making in humans, to OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer model family. The results show that as the models expand in size and linguistic proficiency they increasingly display human-like intuitive system 1 thinking and associated cognitive errors. This pattern shifts notably with the introduction of ChatGPT models, which tend to respond correctly, avoiding the traps embedded in the tasks. Both ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 utilize the input-output context window to engage in chain-of-thought reasoning, reminiscent of how people use notepads to support their system 2 thinking. Yet, they remain accurate even when prevented from engaging in chain-of-thought reasoning, indicating that their system-1-like next-word generation processes are more accurate than those of older models. Our findings highlight the value of applying psychological methodologies to study large language models, as this can uncover previously undetected emergent characteristics.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
